summary: The document describes the Applicant's suite of erosion and sediment control measures, monitoring programs, and flow augmentation proposals that respond to the concerns raised by Boyne and Ingram, including benthic sampling programs, sediment traps, silt fences, seeding of disturbed slopes, and post-operational monitoring of Howard Creek.
text:
The Applicant proposes to concentrate construction activities within the Bad Creek and West Bad Creek drainage basin to minimize adverse impacts on Howard Creek. Applicant estimates that nearly all the earth and rock fill material for construction of the dams could be obtained from within the reservoir basin area, thus eliminating the use of extensive areas west of South Carolina Route 171.
The permanent access road and temporary construction roads would be routed to minimize silt-laden runoff into existing streams and would emphasize a route within the Bad Creek drainage basin. Slopes would be seeded as soon as possible after land disturbances, and temporary roads would be regraded and p<sup>1</sup> inted as soon as they are no longer needed. Drainage control measures would be taken in areas where runoff would drain outside the Bad Creek drainage basin. The construction yard area would be located so as to take advantage of topographic features; natural slopes would be left undisturbed while other portions would be terraced, sloped, and drained to minimize siltation. Strips of existing trees and ground cover would be left intact. Contractor shops and staging areas would be situated in designated locations with consideration given to the environmental impact. Disturbed areas would be kept as small as possible

Measures are being taken by the Applicant in the Bad Creek and West Bad Creek drainage basins to control erosion resulting from initial exploratory excavations and disruptions at the upper reservoir site. These measures include gates to keep out vehicle traffic and silt fences, "Hold-Gro" erosion control fabric, and planting of fast-growing ground covers (Figures 4-1 thru 4-4). Continual maintenance efforts would be necessary to ensure the success of the measures taken.
Applicant has developed an erosion and sediment pollution control plan to be implemented during construction of the project (Appendix B) to protect the Howard Creek drainage, the Whitewater River, and the Whitewater arm of Lake Jocassee. Control measures would be taken to reduce erosion from construction of project facilities and appurtenant structures. The plan includes measures to control erosion and siltation into the Whitewater River basin should the supplemental borrow area shown in Figure 1-4 be required. The plan also includes post-construction measures, including grading, planting of ground covers, and closing of roads no longer in use.
Retaining walls and cofferdams would be constructed to control runoff and siltation during construction of the tunnel adits, excavation of the power tunnel and powerhouse chamber, and construction of the underground facilities.
Sediment traps would be placed in the old stream beds in the upper reservoir area during land clearing operations and dam construction, to help contain suspended solids within the project area. Additionally, the diversion intake structure would create a settling basin behind the main dam. Water breaks and soil catchment basins would also be used to control runoff. If needed, a major settlement basin would be placed in Bad Creek, downstream from the dam site, to further minimize siltation and turbidity in Howard Creek. The scheduling and conduct of the reservoir clearing would also minimize siltation in Howard Creek. The flow of West Bad Creek would be diverted to Bad Creek before the initiation of clearing in the West Bad Creek basin. Riprap material would be placed on both faces of the dams and dike to control erosion.
Routing, access, and construction of transmission lines would be carried out with consideration towards minimizing environmental impacts. Access would be gained through use of existing roads or by construction of

temporary ones. Tower sites would be cleared locally for construction and safe operation, then terraced where practical to reduce erosion. No tree trimming would be done. Some forest lands along the proposed Bad Creek-to-Oconee line right-of-way would be cleared to maintain proper line clearance. In mountainous terrain, selective clearing would be used to the fullest extent possible to maintain line clearance, and long-span towers would be used to cross valleys between mountain ridges, alleviating the need to clear all vegetation from beneath the lines. Applicant states that the present data show that they would be able to span the entire Howard Creek ravine with the proposed transmission line, thus minimizing the impact on water quality. Where forest lands are cleared, the Applicant would fertilize and revegetate transmission line right-of-way immediately with plants such as fesque, German millet, sericea lespedeza, and other vegetation suitable as cover and as food for wildlife.
Where the 525-kV line parallels or crosses Lake Keowee and streams, towers would be located far enough away from the water's edge to avoid runoff problems.
Low growing vegetation at the water's edge would not be disturbed, thus maintaining soil stability. In the more mountainous area near Bad Creek, forested areas on both sides of the streams would be left intact to maintain watershed protection.
In planning the Bad Creek transmission facilities, the use of common corridors for multiple lines has been planned to reduce the number of right-of-way corridors.
Solid and liquid construction wastes would be handled in accordance with applicable Government regulations. Care would be taken to prohibit the discharge of any undesirable chemicals or wastes during the operation of the project.
During construction of the project dams, water from the Bad Creek basin would be routed through a pipe beneath the main dam and would flow down the remaining 600 to 700 feet of Bad Creek, emptying into Howard Creek.
Applicant proposes to construct a flow augmentation system with a multilevel intake in the upper reservoir. The intake levels would be at elevations of 2,280, 2,230, and 2,120 feet (30, 80, and 190 feet below full pool elevation, respectively). The discharge would be through an aeration device at the base of the Bad Creek Dam. The intake located

at elevation 2,120 feet would be about 30 feet below maximum drawdown. The augmentation system would be capable of delivering flows of up to 15 cfs, an amount that would more than restore Howard Creek to preproject base flow levels. The use of this system would be dependent upon the quality of the water available in the upper reservoir to use for augmentation.
Environmental studies of streams in the project area have been conducted by Applicant in the areas of hydrology, water quality, benthos, amphibians and reptiles, geology, and recreation and esthetics. An analysis of the Howar. Creek fishery has been made by the South Carolina Department of Wildlife and Marine Resources. Wildlife and botanical studies have also been made by the Applicant. Applicant has sponsored a number of studies of Howard Creek basin in preparation for the development of the proposed Project (Section 2.2.2.2). Applicant has also sponsored or conducted studies of the effect of pumped storage on Lake Jocassee and the trout resources of Howard Creek (Appendices J and K, Exhibit W). Applicant is conducting a study on the vertical distribution of fishes in Lake Jocassee.
